new_statements.relation_note: In the grammatical comparison of the Bongo-Baka 'Jur' dialects (Nyamusa and Molo among the tabulated rows), subject pronouns are usually taken from the emphatic set, first person is a verbal prefix, and second person is usually marked by a tone change on the verb root - i.e. these dialects use grammatical tone on the verb. Nothing about word stress surfaced in any snippet (about 45 probes across three passes; absence in snippet view proves nothing).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-person subject is (usually) expressed by a tone change on the verb root across the compared Bongo-Baka dialects, which include Nyamusa and Molo; grammatical tone, no stress rule stated.
new_statements.exceptions: hedged 'usually' - the snippet does not say which of the dialects (Mo'da, Morokodo, Nyamusa, Molo, Wira, Modo, Lori, Sopi, 'Beli) depart from the tone-change pattern
new_statements.identity_note: PASS-1 WORK, added: a tone statement that neither PRIOR (pass1_statements empty) nor A registered, located in text already on (pass-1 altcopy snippet file, queries q5/q15) and widened/page-fixed by my own GData phrase probes (new file below). Identity: Google Books volume WOA_AQAAIAAJ 'Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages' 1997 (library-bound set starting with No. 7); the snippet carries the article's running head 'Bongo - Baka Grouping 25' = p. 25 of Persson 1997 (pp. 19-39), sec. 4 'Grammatical comparison', immediately after the pronoun feature table whose rows are Mo'da, Morokodo, Nyamusa, Molo, Wira, Modo, Lori, Sopi, 'Beli. Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description ref 82116 for nyam1279. Access 'open' refers to the snippet view; the PDF at sil.org is nominally open but an automated-access block-403 to every non-browser attempt (10 tries held by the project).

readall_conflicts: No source opened says anything about stress in Nyamusa-Molo itself, so there is no conflict about this language. Between the two related sources there is a disagreement worth recording: Tucker & Bryan 1966's group-level Bongo-Bagirmi remark puts stress on the first syllable of disyllables (based on Bongo, Baka, Morokodo, Kresh, Yulu, Kara, Sara Mbai), whereas Persson 1981's first-hand description of the closely related Mödö dialect of Jur Modo (same Jur dialect cluster as Nyamusa) finds penultimate word stress with final stress on disyllabic VCV verbs and initial stress on HHH/LLL trisyllabic nouns. Neither can be transferred to Nyamusa without data.
